Realistically, that is a pipe dream.

Marcelo, my next column is about passion. So tell me, honestly: what are you really hooked on?
Old soul, without a doubt. I have been a sucker for a good horn section since I was fifteen. Some of those records still give me goosebumps.
That is lovely. And football? A friend told me you are a die-hard fan.
I am. When my team won the title, I was over the moon. The stadium was so electric that nobody sat down for ninety minutes. Sorry, I am getting carried away.
Do not apologize. Your enthusiasm is infectious. But for the column I need the why. Why does soul strike a chord with you?
Because it is utterly honest. Those singers lived and breathed every word. It was such a different world from mine, and yet it felt like home.

Hi Marcelo, it is Fiona. I listened to our interview again last night, and honestly, it was absolutely brilliant. My editor says your answer about soul music is the best part of the piece. She would like a photo of you with your records, if that is all right with you. One more thing. You told me that old disco is your guilty pleasure, and I laughed so much that I almost dropped my phone. Can I put that in the column too? If you say no, that is totally fine. Oh, and I am going to a match in Liverpool on Saturday. I am not a die-hard fan, but I hear the atmosphere is so electric that people lose their voices. Call me back when you can.

Welcome back to The Long Game. Today, a question from a listener in Brazil. He writes: when I talk about music in English, I sound like a weather report. Here is the problem, and it is extremely common. Most learners use one intensifier for everything: very. Very good, very nice, very interesting. Nothing is wrong with it, but it is utterly flat. So try this. First, keep very for normal adjectives, like good or tired. Second, when the feeling is bigger, change the adjective, not the volume. Do not say very good. Say brilliant, and if you mean it, absolutely brilliant. Third, give one detail. Passion is in the detail: the horn section in the second verse, the goal in the ninetieth minute. And finally, watch the person in front of you. If their eyes are glazing over, you are getting carried away. Enthusiasm is infectious, but only for about two minutes.

First, Fiona meets a friend in a tiny record shop in São Paulo, a die-hard fan who has been hooked on soul since he was fifteen. Then the friend describes the music in English as very good, and his words sound utterly flat. After that, Fiona explains that some adjectives, like good, take very, but extreme ones, like brilliant, take absolutely. Next, she watches a match in Liverpool with a fan whose stadium is so electric that it gives him goosebumps. Finally, she tells readers to say that what they love is absolutely amazing, and to tell people why.
